body.heading: Water, soap and movement
paragraphs: Washing is a partnership between chemistry and movement. Detergent molecules have a water-loving end and a grease-loving end, so they surround particles of oil and dirt and lift them off fabric, letting the water carry them away.

But soap alone is slow. The machine adds mechanical action: the drum turns so that clothes are repeatedly lifted and dropped through the soapy water, flexing the fabric and working the solution through the fibres where the dirt hides. Front-loading machines tumble clothes through a shallow pool of water; top-loaders stir them with a central agitator or impeller instead — the choreography differs, but the principle does not.

body.heading: The wash cycle, step by step
paragraphs: A typical cycle fills the drum with water, adds detergent, and tumbles the load for several minutes. The dirty water drains away, fresh water rinses the soap and loosened dirt out — sometimes twice — and then comes the spin.

In the spin, the drum rotates at speeds that can exceed a thousand revolutions per minute. The clothes are pinned to the drum wall while the water, free to move, escapes through the drum's holes and is pumped away — the same effect that flings rain off a spinning umbrella.

body.heading: Why loads go unbalanced
paragraphs: A single heavy, waterlogged towel can unbalance the drum, and modern machines sense the wobbling and redistribute the load or slow the spin to protect themselves. The shaking of an unbalanced load shows how much energy a fast-spinning drum carries.

For all the electronics, the basic recipe is unchanged from the washboard era: soak, agitate, rinse, wring. The machine simply does the agitating and wringing far more patiently than any pair of hands.

description: Soap loosens the dirt, tumbling works it free, and a fast spin flings the water out of the clothes.
